## You're teaching, not presenting {.dark background-color="#022F4A"}

[A presentation ends when you stop talking. **A training ends when they can do it.**]{.statement}

<br>

[Every team owes one. Pick something your project needs, and you'll learn it properly by teaching it.]{.orange}

## The shape of a training

::: {.flow}
::: {.box .hl}
Frame the need
:::

[→]{.arrow}

::: {.box .hl}
Navigate to details
:::

[→]{.arrow}

::: {.box}
Give examples
:::

[→]{.arrow}

::: {.box}
Let them practice
:::

[→]{.arrow}

::: {.box}
Review / reflect
:::
:::

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
**Slides** carry the first two steps.
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
**Code** carries the next two.
:::
:::

[Frame all of it the way **industry** would: why a team would pay for this skill.]{.orange}

## 1 · Frame the need

**One slide. Why should anyone in this room care?**

- What problem does this solve that we currently solve badly, or not at all?
- Where does it show up in **our project**?
- What breaks without it?

::: {.takeaway}
**If you can't name the need, don't teach the tool.** Nobody remembers a solution to a problem they never felt.
:::

## 2 · Navigate to details

**Enough background to follow along, and no more.**

- The two or three ideas they must hold to read your code
- The vocabulary, defined once
- Where it sits next to what we already know

[Resist teaching the whole API. **You are not the documentation.**]{.orange}

## 3 · Give examples

**Working code they can read, on data they recognize.**

- Start with the smallest version that does something real
- Show the output, not just the code
- Use **our C-Store data** where you can, so nobody is learning a new dataset at the same time
- Build up in steps: one idea per cell

## 4 · Let them practice

**This is the part teams skip. It's the part that works.**

::: {.cards}
::: {.card}
[Make it runnable]{.card-title}

A notebook in our GitHub org, or a Databricks notebook they can clone.
:::
::: {.card}
[Make it small]{.card-title}

Ten minutes, with a clear finish line. Not a project.
:::
::: {.card}
[Make it graded by them]{.card-title}

Give the expected output, so they know whether they got it.
:::
:::

**Walk the room while they work.** Where they get stuck is your real feedback.

## 5 · Review and reflect

**Close the loop.**

- What should they be able to do now that they couldn't before?
- The one mistake you'd bet most of them made
- Where to look next: docs, a guide, the book chapter

## What good looks like

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.card}
[DataCamp is the model]{.card-title}

Short video, immediate coding, repeat. Never more than a few minutes of talking before you do something.
:::
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.card}
[AI study guides]{.card-title}

Fine for building your material and checking your explanation.

**Not** a substitute for writing the practice activity yourself.
:::
:::
:::

## Your checklist

- A **need** stated in one sentence
- **Slides** for the first two steps, short
- **Runnable code** in our GitHub org, self-contained
- A **practice activity** with an expected output
- A **takeaway** slide and somewhere to go next
- A dry run — **time it**

::: {.takeaway}
**Copy `topics/_training_template.qmd`** to start. It has these five sections and the course theme already set up.
:::
